Other 82% hits (KPMG: competitive landscape within 24 months; CSA: unknown agents) are about unrelated subjects.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "82% agree AI agents will change how they write infrastructure within 12 months survey"; "Pulumi State of Agentic Infrastructure 2026 82% change how they write infrastructure"; top results didn't address the claim (closest: https://www.pulumi.com/state-of-agentic-infrastructure/)
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim names no source, and the likely Pulumi survey uses a six-month horizon, not 12 months. Also, a 2026 survey stat is being added to a post titled "trends shaping 2024." Check where the 82% comes from.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi's 2026 survey, 63% say they trust agents to make production changes, yet manual approval remains close to universal today.

Claim: "63% ... trust agents to make production changes, yet manual approval remains close to universal". The claim paraphrases the source without changing its meaning.

verdicts.text: - Teams expecting agents to generate half or more of their infrastructure code rise from **45% today to 52%** within six months.

verdicts.framing_note: The source's "50% or more ... in six months" means the same as the claim's "half or more ... within six months."
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim cites a 2026 survey, but it sits in a post whose slug is '...trends-shaping-2024-and-beyond'. The dates are worth checking. The source is Pulumi's own survey report, which is the primary source but not independent of Pulumi.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi blog post 'The Agentic Infrastructure Era' exists and argues AIOps is headed toward a supervised agentic operating model rather than faster dashboards and alerting alone.

That page returned 200 and only describes Neo ("Meet Neo, our AI-powered infrastructure engineering agent"). The fetched excerpt never mentions that blog post or its argument about AIOps.

verdicts.text: According to Mordor Intelligence, the global Kubernetes market is valued at USD 3.13 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 8.41 billion by 2031, a 21.85% CAGR.
verdicts.evidence: The pre-fetch of the cited Mordor Intelligence page returned HTTP 403 Forbidden with an empty body, so I could not check the USD 3.13B (2026), USD 8.41B (2031) or 21.85% CAGR figures. A 403 from a commercial research site usually means it blocks automated fetchers, not that the page is gone, so I did not treat it as a dead link.
verdicts.framing_note: No passage was fetched, so the framing could not be checked.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The numbers are internally consistent: 3.13 × 1.2185^5 ≈ 8.41. A 403 is most likely bot-blocking, so a web search should be able to confirm the current figures.

verdicts.text: CNCF's Q3 2025 report says 30% of backend developers now use Kubernetes directly, down from a peak of 36% in Q3 2023, a decline the report attributes to the technology's growing maturity.

I couldn't find a passage to confirm the 30% / 36% figures, the "backend developers" group, or the maturity explanation, so I have no quote to check the framing against.
verdicts.framing_note: Couldn't classify: no text could be pulled from the PDF body.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim bundles several points, and each could drift from the source: a specific group ("backend developers" vs. all developers), a peak-and-decline trend, and a cause credited to the report ("attributes to growing maturity"). The cause in particular may be the author's reading, not the report's. A human should read the PDF text to check.

verdicts.text: Inference workloads powered by LLMs and GPUs now require low-latency execution closer to the user, pushing organizations to schedule AI pipelines across edge and core clusters, often using Kubernetes as the common control plane.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Several industry sources back the general trend. A 2025 survey quotes a practitioner: "For low-latency inference, edge-deployed Kubernetes clusters are still the best fit." Microsoft's AKS/Arc blog describes using "the same Kubernetes APIs, deployment patterns, and lifecycle workflows across cloud and non‑cloud environments" to keep inference close to the data. These are vendor and blog sources, not measurements, so the support is circumstantial.
verdicts.source: https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/08/14/ai-in-kubernetes-operations/; https://blog.aks.azure.com/2026/04/07/ai-inference-on-aks-arc-part-1; WebSearch ran query "Kubernetes edge AI inference low latency control plane edge and core clusters"
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Inference workloads ... now require" low-latency edge execution is too broad. Many LLM inference workloads run centrally in the cloud. Only latency-sensitive workloads need edge placement, so a hedge like "increasingly" or "latency-sensitive" would make it accurate.

verdicts.text: Pulumi has published a comparison of Kubernetes IaC tools at /blog/best-kubernetes-iac-tools-2026/.

That page returned HTTP 200 with the title "Beyond YAML in Kubernetes: The 2026 Automation Era | Pulumi Blog", and the truncated body is only site navigation, so nothing in it confirms or denies the linked comparison post.
verdicts.framing_note: The cited URL is a different post from the one the claim names (/blog/best-kubernetes-iac-tools-2026/), so no framing check was run against it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A quick check of the repo for content/blog/best-kubernetes-iac-tools-2026/ would settle whether this internal link works.

verdicts.text: Kubernetes is evolving to support AI through GPU-aware scheduling and more advanced workload orchestration.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Several sources say Kubernetes has added GPU-aware scheduling through Dynamic Resource Allocation (GA in 1.34) and workload-aware scheduling features. One says "Kubernetes v1.36... introduced further workload-aware scheduling capabilities including PodGroups, topology-aware scheduling, workload-aware preemption."
verdicts.framing_note: This is a general industry-trend claim with no cited source. Several independent 2026 articles back it up, but none of them is an official kubernetes.io page.

verdicts.text: AI-powered coding assistants like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor have moved from novelty to everyday tooling for a large share of enterprise software teams.

That backs the qualitative claim that these tools are now everyday tooling for a large share of professional teams.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim cites no source and makes a qualitative point, not a numeric one. The surveys measure professional developers in general, not enterprise teams specifically. That doesn't really change the "large share" wording.

verdicts.text: According to Gartner, 63% of organizations are currently piloting, deploying or beginning to use AI code assistants.

The source is a survey of 598 respondents in Q3 2023. The 63% figure and the Gartner attribution are correct, but the third category is paraphrased from "have already deployed" to "beginning to use".
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says 'piloting, deploying or have already deployed' and the claim says 'piloting, deploying or beginning to use'. The claim describes a finished deployment as early adoption. It also drops the survey scope (598 global respondents, Q3 2023).

verdicts.evidence: The cited page loaded (HTTP 200), but it is the MCP 2026-07-28 specification release announcement. It covers protocol changes ("a stateless protocol core, Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing...") and SDK download numbers, but nothing in the fetched text says enterprise expectations for AI assistants are rising, or that assistants must understand infrastructure state and security posture.

verdicts.text: Pulumi released Pulumi Agent Skills, a collection of infrastructure expertise packaged for use in AI coding assistants such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI, reducing hallucination and improving outputs.

It lists Claude Code and Cursor, and says it "works with Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, and other agent tools." The README does not name Gemini CLI, and it makes no claim about reducing hallucination.

verdicts.text: Pulumi has a Remote MCP Server that provides infrastructure access for AI assistants, and Pulumi Neo executes actions with previews, policies, and orchestration.

The Neo docs say Neo "can run `pulumi preview` to validate a change, surface policy violations" and "adds organizational context, policy guardrails, human-in-the-loop approvals". Calling this "orchestration" is fair, since the same announcement describes Neo doing "multi-step planning" and "managing the entire workflow".
verdicts.framing_note: The claim's wording is a light paraphrase: Neo "executes actions with previews, policies, and orchestration" versus the docs' "runs previews", "policy guardrails", and "multi-step planning".

verdicts.text: Modern IaC, unified governance, reusable components, and policy frameworks are all core capabilities of the Pulumi Cloud platform.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi docs index lists these as product areas: "Discovery & governance — Search, compliance, and policy enforcement across your cloud infrastructure" and "Internal Developer Platform — Self-service infrastructure with templates, guardrails". Together with Pulumi IaC and components/private registry, this covers the four capabilities the claim names. Loosely, "modern IaC" belongs to Pulumi IaC, which works alongside Pulumi Cloud rather than being part of it, but it's a fair marketing summary.
